lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, History is the story of people like us. Today, we step through the last door. Whoosh! Hot wind blows on our faces. Golden sand dunes roll on and on under a huge blue sky. Then something pops out of a hole in the sand. It's a tiny fox with enormous ears! He says, Hi there! I'm Fen, a fennec fox. Welcome to the Desert of the Sun! Kiko looks up and asks, Will it rain later? Fen laughs. Rain? It hardly ever rains here. Hardly ever（ほとんど ～ない） means almost never. Say it with me. It hardly ever rains here. Wonderful! Then Fen gives us a shiny golden compass. It's the Sun Compass! It has six empty slots around the edge. Fen opens his little guidebook. Let's read the first page. "Welcome to the Desert of the Sun! A desert is a very dry place. It gets less than about two hundred fifty millimeters of rain in a whole year. Some deserts are hot, but some are cold. In fact, the largest desert in the world is icy Antarctica! Here, it hardly ever rains, so plants and animals must be clever to survive. Keep the Sun Compass with you. Each time you finish an important part of your journey, a sun crystal will fill one of its six slots. When all six shine, the compass will show you the way to your next adventure." How much rain does a desert get? Less than about two hundred fifty millimeters a year. What is the largest desert in the world? Antarctica. Now, phonics. Today's word part is g, e, o, geo. Geo means the earth. Geography. Graphy means write or draw, so geography is the study of places on Earth. Geology. Logy means study. Geology is the study of rocks and the ground. Geometry. Metry means measure. Geometry is the study of shapes. Next time, we will camp in the desert and feel a hot day and a very cold night!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, It hardly ever rains here. Today, Fen leads us to a little camp between two sand dunes. The afternoon sun is burning, and the sand is too hot to touch. Haru looks at the thermometer. Wow! It's forty-two degrees! We sit in the shade of the tent and drink lots of water. Then the sun goes down. The sky turns orange, pink, and purple. Soon, thousands of stars come out, but we start to shiver. Brr! Now we need jackets and blankets! Fen says, In the desert, it's very hot during the day, but cold at night. Say it with me. It's very hot during the day, but cold at night. Great! Riko asks, Why does it get so cold? Fen explains. The air here is very dry, and there are no clouds. Clouds and wet air work like a blanket. Without them, the heat of the day escapes into the sky. Before bed, Haru writes in his diary. Let's read it. "Day One in the Desert. This afternoon, it was over forty degrees. My water bottle felt like hot tea! We stayed in the shade and didn't run around. At sunset, everything changed. The wind became cool, and the temperature dropped very fast. Fen says desert nights can get close to zero degrees. Now I'm wearing my jacket, two pairs of socks, and a hat. But the stars are amazing. I have never seen so many stars in my life!" How hot was it in the afternoon? Over forty degrees. Why is Haru wearing two pairs of socks? Because the night is very cold. Now, phonics. Geo means the earth, and today we meet some geo people. Geographer. Add e, r to geography, and it means a person who studies geography. Geologist. A geologist studies rocks and the ground. Geoscientist. A geoscientist studies the whole Earth, its land, water, and air. Next time, we will find water in the middle of the desert!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, It's very hot during the day, but cold at night. Today, we walk across the desert with Fen. Crunch, crunch. Kiko is surprised. The ground here isn't soft sand. It's hard rock and small stones called gravel. Fen says, Many people think deserts are all sand, but most of the Sahara is rock and gravel. Then Haru shouts, Look! Trees! In front of us, there are tall palm trees, green grass, and a small blue pond. Birimo rubs his eyes. Is it a dream? Fen says, No, it's an oasis! An oasis is a place where water comes out. Say it with me. An oasis is a place where water comes out. Perfect! Riko asks, But where does the water come from? It hardly ever rains here. Fen points down at his feet. It comes from under the ground. Next to the pond, there is a wooden sign. Let's read it. "Welcome to the Oasis! You are standing at a place where water comes out of the ground. Deep under the sand and rocks, there is water. Here, it rises up as a spring. People also dig wells to get it. Thanks to this water, date palms grow tall, and their sweet fruit has fed travelers for thousands of years. Please keep the water clean, and never waste it. Every drop is a gift." Where does the water at the oasis come from? From under the ground. What trees grow at the oasis? Date palms. Now, phonics. Today, geo meets some new friends. Geothermal. Thermal means heat, so geothermal means the heat inside the earth. Japan's hot springs get their heat from inside the earth. Geopark. A geopark is a park where you can learn about the earth, like rocks, volcanoes, and coasts. Geoglyph. A geoglyph is a giant picture drawn on the ground. The Nazca Lines in Peru are famous geoglyphs. Next time, Fen will show us a big climate map of the whole world!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, An oasis is a place where water comes out. Today, a strong wind is blowing sand everywhere, so we stay inside Fen's big tent. Fen rolls out a huge map of the world. It's covered in colors: yellow, green, white, and dark green. Fen says, This is my climate map. Climate means the usual weather in a place over many years. Haru points to the dark green part. What's the weather like here? Fen says, That's the rainforest. It's hot and rainy all year. Some places are rainy all year. Say it with me. Some places are rainy all year. Wonderful! Kiko finds Japan. It's light green. Fen says, Some places have four seasons, like Japan. Let's read the key on the map. "Climate Map Key. Dark green: rainforest. It is hot and rainy all year, and tall trees grow very close together. The Amazon rainforest in South America is the largest one. Yellow: desert. It is dry all year. Some deserts, like the Sahara, are hot. Others, like the Gobi in Asia, have very cold winters. Light green: four seasons. Summers are warm, winters are cool or cold, and it rains in many months. White: polar. It is freezing all year, and the land is covered with ice and snow." What's the weather like in the rainforest? It's hot and rainy all year. Which desert has very cold winters? The Gobi. Is this a fact or an opinion? Japan has the best climate in the world. Riko thinks so, but it's an opinion! Now, phonics. Today, geo words get new endings. Geographic. Add i, c, and geography becomes a describing word. A geographic map shows mountains, rivers, and deserts. Geometric. Geometric shapes are circles, triangles, and squares. Look, Fen's tent has a geometric pattern! Geode. A geode is a round rock. It looks plain on the outside, but inside, it's full of sparkling crystals. Next time, we will give a climate report about deserts around the world!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The Sahara is located in North Africa. It's hot and dry. Today, we hear bells. Ding, ding, ding. A long line of camels is walking over the dunes. It's a caravan! At the front, there is a big old camel with a gentle smile. He kneels down slowly and says, Good morning, little travelers. I'm Humphrey. I lead this caravan. Hop on! We climb onto the camels. Whoa! They stand up back legs first, and we almost fall off! Later, Haru asks, Humphrey, aren't you thirsty? Humphrey smiles. Not yet. Camels can go many days without water. Say it with me. Camels can go many days without water. Great! Kiko asks, Is there water in your hump? Humphrey shakes his head. Our humps store fat, not water. Humphrey carries a fact card in his saddle bag. Let's read it. "Camel Fact Card. Camels are amazing desert travelers. They can go about a week or more without water. When they finally find water, they can drink about one hundred liters at one time! Their humps store fat, not water. Long eyelashes protect their eyes, and they can close their noses to keep sand out. Their wide feet don't sink in soft sand. They also have tough mouths, so they can eat thorny desert plants. Some people call camels the ships of the desert." How much water can a camel drink at one time? About one hundred liters. What do camels' humps store? Fat. Is this a fact or an opinion? Camels are the best animals in the world. It's an opinion, but Humphrey likes it! Now, phonics. Today's ending is a, l. Al turns a word into a describing word. Nature, natural. Drop the e, and the sound changes from nay to na. Nation, national. Nay becomes na again. Tropic, tropical. Tropical places are hot and wet. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Camels can go many days without water. Today, Humphrey's caravan stops near some big rocks. Fen whispers, Shh. Let's watch the desert animals. A little lizard runs quickly across the hot sand. Then Riko looks at Fen. Fen, why are your ears so big? Fen laughs. My ears are my air conditioners! Heat leaves my body through them. Desert foxes have big ears so that they can stay cool. So that（～できるように） means for this reason, or to make something possible. Say it with me. Desert foxes have big ears so that they can stay cool. Perfect! Fen turns his ears this way and that way. They help me hear bugs moving under the sand, too. Dinner! Haru asks, Why are your feet so furry? Fen says, So that I can walk on hot sand. Let's read a page from Fen's animal notebook. "How Desert Animals Survive. I'm a fennec fox, the smallest fox in the world. My huge ears let heat out of my body so that I can stay cool. They also help me hear insects under the sand. My feet are covered with fur so that I can walk on hot sand. During the day, I sleep in a cool burrow under the ground. At night, when the air is cooler, I go out to hunt. My friend Humphrey has long eyelashes so that sand can't get into his eyes." Why does Fen have furry feet? So that he can walk on hot sand. When does Fen hunt? At night. Now, phonics. Let's add a, l again. Coast, coastal. A coastal town is a town by the sea. Season, seasonal. Seasonal fruit comes only in one season, like watermelon in summer. Center, central. Drop the e from e, r, and add a, l. Central means in the middle. Fen's burrow has a central room, and it's cool inside! Next time, we will visit a garden of tall, spiky cactus plants!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Desert foxes have big ears so that they can stay cool. Today, Fen takes us to a cactus garden. Some cactus plants are round like balls. Some are flat like pancakes. And one is taller than a house! Its green arms point up to the sky. Haru touches a spine. Ouch! Fen laughs. Be careful! Then Fen points to a thick green stem. It's full of water inside, like a sponge. A cactus stores water in its thick stem. Say it with me. A cactus stores water in its thick stem. Wonderful! Kiko asks, But where are its leaves? Fen points to the spines. Its spines are special leaves. Riko asks, Why does a cactus have spines? Fen says, To lose less water and to keep animals away. Let's read the sign in front of the tallest cactus. "The Saguaro Cactus. This giant can grow taller than twelve meters and live for more than one hundred fifty years. Like other cactus plants, it stores water in its thick stem. After a rain, the stem gets fatter. Its spines are special leaves. They lose much less water than big flat leaves, they protect the cactus from hungry animals, and they even make a little shade. Waxy skin keeps the water inside. The roots are wide and shallow, so they can catch rain quickly before it dries up." How tall can a saguaro grow? Taller than twelve meters. What do the spines do? They lose less water, protect the cactus, and make a little shade. Now, phonics. A, l makes describing words. Globe, global. Drop the e and add a, l. Global means all around the world. Culture, cultural. Drop the e again. Cultural things are about the way people live, like food and festivals. Origin, original. An original idea is new, your very own. The cactus has an original way to save water! Next time, the Sun Compass will show us pictures of icy lands!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, A cactus stores water in its thick stem. Today, the Sun Compass starts to glow. A picture appears in the air above it. It's white and icy! In the picture, emperor penguins stand on the ice in Antarctica. Fen says, Penguins have thick feathers to keep warm. Say it with me. Penguins have thick feathers to keep warm. Great! Look! The penguins are standing very close together. Emperor penguins huddle together in order to keep warm. In order to means the same as to here, but it sounds a little more formal. Then the picture changes to the Arctic. An Arctic fox is walking in the snow. Fen says, Look at its ears! They're so small! Let's read the card under the picture. "Animals in Cold Places. Emperor penguins live in Antarctica. They have thick, tightly packed feathers and a layer of fat to keep warm. In storms, they huddle together in order to share their heat. Polar bears live in the Arctic. Their thick fur, black skin, and a layer of fat keep the cold out. The Arctic fox has small ears and thick fur to keep heat in. In winter, its fur turns white, so it can hide in the snow. Desert animals let heat out. Cold-place animals keep heat in." Why do emperor penguins huddle together? In order to share their heat. What color is the Arctic fox's fur in winter? White. Fen laughs. My ears let heat out, and its ears keep heat in. We're cousins with opposite ears! Now, phonics. More a, l words! Its long eyelashes keep sand out of its eyes, and it can close its nose in a sandstorm. It can go many days without water, and its hump stores fat, not water. Its tough mouth can even eat thorny plants. Some people call it the ship of the desert. Can you guess? Hint: he leads our caravan!" What helps this animal walk on soft sand? Its wide feet. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The mountains are located in the north. Today, Fen rolls a giant globe into the tent. It's as tall as Birimo! Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, and Australia. There are seven continents. Say it with me. There are seven continents. Perfect! Asia is the largest continent. Haru finds Japan. It's a small island country to the east of Asia. Kiko asks, How many oceans are there? Fen says, There are five. The Pacific is the largest. Let's read the little guidebook that comes with the globe. "Our Blue and Green Planet. There are seven continents and five oceans on Earth. The oceans are the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern, and the Arctic. The Pacific Ocean is so big that all the continents could fit inside it. Africa is home to the Sahara, the largest hot desert in the world. Antarctica is covered with ice, but it's a desert, too, because very little snow or rain falls there. In fact, it's the largest desert on Earth!" Which ocean is the largest? The Pacific. Why is Antarctica a desert? Because very little snow or rain falls there. Now, phonics. W, a, r, d means toward. It sounds like word, but we spell it w, a, r, d. Northward. Southward. Eastward. Westward. If you fly eastward from Japan, you cross the Pacific Ocean and reach North America. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The graph shows the temperature in July. Today, Dr. Mira takes us to the gate of Sunrise Desert Park. Did it go up or down here? Dr. Mira says, It decreased a little in the stormy year. There were many big sandstorms, so fewer people came. Then Haru finds another graph. The number of camels in the park stayed the same, about fifty every year. Let's read the park's report. "Sunrise Desert Park: Ten Years of Visitors. Ten years ago, the park was very quiet. Only two hundred fifty thousand people visited. Then the park opened a star-watching tour and a camel trail, and more and more people came. Three years ago, there were many sandstorms, and the number of visitors decreased a little. But last year, one million people visited! Now the park asks everyone to stay on the trails so that the desert plants stay safe." How many people visited ten years ago? Two hundred fifty thousand. Why did more people come? About seventy percent of Earth's surface is water. Let's read the poster next to the whiteboard. "Our Water Planet. About seventy percent of Earth's surface is water, but almost all of it is salty sea water. Only about three percent of Earth's water is fresh water, and most of that is frozen ice. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This graph shows the rain in our desert town. As you can see, it hardly ever rains in summer. Today, Fen leads us across the hot sand to Palm Village. In the middle of the village, there is an old stone well. A long line of people waits beside it with buckets and clay jars. An old woman slowly pulls up the rope. Splash! Cool, clear water fills her bucket. Nobody spills a drop. Fen's big ears twitch. He whispers, Here, every drop counts. Water is precious in the desert. Say it with me. Water is precious in the desert. Wonderful! Precious means very important and hard to get, like treasure. Riko asks, Why is water so precious? Fen says, It hardly ever rains here. Let's read the sign next to the well. "Welcome to the Palm Village Well. This well is very old and very deep. The water comes from under the ground, far below the sand. Our village gets less than 100 millimeters of rain a year, so this well is our life. Please take only what you need. Close the lid after you use the well, so that sand and animals stay out. Thank you for helping us. Water is precious, so let's not waste a single drop!" Where does the water come from? From under the ground. Why should you close the lid? So that sand and animals stay out. Is this a fact or an opinion? Water is precious. It's an opinion, but in the desert, everyone shares it! Now, phonics. Today's ending is a, g, e. It sounds like idge, but we spell it a, g, e. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Water is precious in the desert. Today, Dr. Mira Sands takes us to Mirror Lake. Long ago, the lake was so smooth and wide that it looked like a giant mirror. But now, we see a ring of white, cracked mud all around it. The water is far away from the old shore. Haru points to a big rock. Look! There's an old water line up here! Dr. Mira nods and shows us her temperature graph. Every summer this lake gets hotter and hotter. The hot sun turns the water into vapor, and it goes up into the air. Because of the heat, the lake became smaller. Say it with me. Because of the heat, the lake became smaller. Great! Because of comes before a thing, like the heat or the rain. Let's read Dr. Mira's notebook. "Mirror Lake Notes. Ten years ago, Mirror Lake was about two kilometers wide. Now, it is less than one kilometer wide. Why? First, the summers here have become hotter. Because of the heat, a lot of water goes up into the air every day. Second, it hardly ever rained this year. Third, more and more farms take water from the lake. Because of the dry weather, many plants on the shore turned brown. The fish and birds have fewer places to live now. We must take care of this lake." How wide was the lake ten years ago? About two kilometers. Give one reason why the lake became smaller. The summers became hotter, it hardly ever rained, or farms took water. Now, phonics. Today's ending is u, r, e. Listen. Temperature. Measure. Pressure. Moisture. The ending sounds like cher, zher, or sher, but we spell it u, r, e. We measure the temperature with a thermometer. Moisture means a little water in the air or in the ground. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Because of the heat, the lake became smaller. Today, Fen takes us over a tall sand dune. At the top, we stop and stare. Below us, there is a green valley full of trees, fields, and flowers! Birds are singing everywhere. Fen says, Welcome to Green Valley. Forty years ago, this place was brown and dusty. Then the people had an idea. People planted trees. As a result, the village became green again. Say it with me. People planted trees. As a result, the village became green again. Perfect! As a result tells us what happened next because of something. Let's read the story board in the village square. "The Story of Green Valley. Forty years ago, Green Valley was dry and brown. Strong winds blew sand into the fields, and the crops died. Many families had to leave. Then the villagers made a plan. They planted long rows of trees around the village. The trees stopped the wind and gave shade. Their roots held the soil in place. As a result, the fields stayed soft and wet, and the crops grew again. Then the birds came back, too. Today, Green Valley is green again!" Why did the crops die? Because of strong winds that blew sand into the fields. What happened after the trees grew? The fields stayed soft and wet, and the crops grew again. Green Valley is a story village, but this happens in the real world, too. In Africa, many countries are planting a Great Green Wall of trees across the Sahel, south of the Sahara, to stop the desert from spreading. Now, phonics. Today's ending is e, a, s, e. It sounds like eess. Increase. Decrease. Release. When the number of trees increases, it goes up. When it decreases, it goes down. Release means let something go. Release the bird, and it flies free! "Lina lived in a small village in the eastern part of a dry valley. It hardly ever rained there, and the old well was almost empty. Every morning, Lina walked for an hour to get water. One day at sunrise, she saw something strange at the dry riverbed. Green plants were growing there, and little birds were hopping around them. But there was no water anywhere. Lina thought, Plants need water. Maybe there is water under the ground! She ran back and told the villagers. They dug and dug. At last, cool water came up. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The graph shows the number of trees in the village. It increased from 100 to 900. Today, Humphrey the old camel leads our farewell caravan. Bells jingle as we sway across the golden dunes. First, we pass our old camp, where the days were hot and the nights were cold. Humphrey turns his long neck and winks. Do camels store water in their humps? Birimo answers, No, you store fat! Haru says, Camels have humps so that they can live without food. Then we stop at Dr. Mira's weather station. Riko points to the thermometer graph. The graph shows how hot it is. Say it with me. Camels have humps so that they can live without food. The graph shows how hot it is. Wonderful! Let's read Kiko's desert journal. "My Desert Journal. We came to the Desert of the Sun through the Corridor of Time. It hardly ever rains here, so water is precious. At the oasis, water comes up from under the ground, and date palms grow there. Fen has big ears so that he can stay cool. A cactus stores water in its thick stem. Mirror Lake became smaller because of the heat. In Green Valley, people planted trees. As a result, the village became green again. I will miss this place!" Why does Fen have big ears? So that he can stay cool. What happened in Green Valley? People planted trees, and the village became green again. Fen gives each of us a round rock. Crack! Inside, it sparkles with crystals. It's a geode! Now, phonics. Let's review. Geode. Geo means earth. Coastal. Coast plus a, l. Northwest. North comes first. Two point five. Two, dot, five. We say point for the dot. Count. O, u, n, t. Let's count our sun crystals. One, two, three, four, five! Next time, it's the World 32 Earth Festival!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Camels have humps so that they can live without food. The graph shows how hot it is. Today is the World 32 Earth Festival at the oasis! Lanterns hang from the palm trees, and drums go boom, boom! Haru, Kiko, and Riko share their maps, posters, and reports. Fen, Humphrey, and Dr. Mira sit in the front row. Then Fen stands up and says, Hot deserts, cold deserts, rainforests, and icy lands. Every place is different. Every place on Earth has its own amazing story. Say it with me. Every place on Earth has its own amazing story. Wonderful! Let's read the festival poster. "Welcome to the World 32 Earth Festival! Visit every stand around the oasis. At the climate stand, you can find out why it hardly ever rains in the desert. At the animal stand, you can learn why camels have wide feet. At the graph stand, you can read reports about water and trees. Don't miss the Save Water Corner! Learn how you can save water by turning off the tap. Thank you for exploring the Desert of the Sun with us!" What can you learn at the animal stand? Why camels have wide feet. Is this a fact or an opinion? Every place on Earth has its own amazing story. It's an opinion, and a wonderful one! Suddenly, the Sun Compass shines like the sun itself. Click! The sixth sun crystal drops in. Congratulations! All six sun crystals are shining! The needle spins, then points to the sea. Far away, we see smoke rising from a volcano. It's the Island of Fire! Now, phonics. Let's review. Geography. Geo means earth. Global. Globe plus a, l. Northern. North plus e, r, n. Three million. Three, then two groups of zero zero zero. No s on million. Average. A, g, e sounds like idge. Goodbye, Fen! Goodbye, Humphrey and Dr. Mira! See you on the Island of Fire!
